title: Graystone Capital - Dedicated capacity discovery
summary: Discovery call to understand Graystone's inference needs and evaluate Redwood Dedicated. Key topics: reserved GPU sizing, network isolation (VPC/on-prem), burst strategy, autoscaling expectations, latency vs cost tradeoffs, security requirements (SOC 2, KMS, SSO). Agreed next steps: Redwood to send sizing + pricing, security pack, and schedule a pilot benchmark with sample prompts.
next_steps: Alex Nguyen - send initial sizing + pricing by 2026-12-02
Priya Shah - share proposed benchmark plan and scripts by 2026-12-03
Jordan Lee - schedule security deep-dive and send SOC2 + network docs by 2026-12-04
action_items: Alex Nguyen: Prepare monthly and committed pricing options and a GPU sizing recommendation - due 2026-12-02
Priya Shah: Draft benchmark test plan (QPS targets, seq length distribution, model variants) - due 2026-12-03
Jordan Lee: Share SOC 2 report, network architecture for VPC peering, and KMS integration notes - due 2026-12-04
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-26 16:00 EST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood CSM), Ethan (Head of ML), Maya (Infra), Tom (CISO)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - I'm Alex, AE on the account, Priya is our SE who will dig into the technical bits, Jordan on CSM. How's everyone doing?
[00:14] Ethan: Good thanks, Ethan here. excited to learn about Dedicated. We run a lot of inference in-house and want to understand the tradeoffs.
[00:22] Maya: Maya from infra — we'll be focussed on isolation, networking, and how bursting would work.
[00:28] Tom: Tom, CISO. I'll ask a few security questions later.
[00:35] Alex: Great. Quick agenda: 1) current stack and pain, 2) workload profile, 3) isolation and security, 4) sizing and burst strategy, 5) next steps. Sound good?
[00:45] Ethan: Yep.

[01:05] Ethan: So to start — we have an internal runtime on prem for most models, but the ops burden is high. Latency varies, cost is high, and supporting multiple model variants is painful. We're exploring Redwood Dedicated because we want reserved capacity and predictable throughput but still need control over data.
[01:30] Priya: Thanks Ethan. When you say latency varies, are we talking tail p95s for small chat-like requests or larger batch generation? And what's your typical token lengths?
[01:42] Ethan: For our customer-facing chat it's short — 20 to 60 tokens typically, p95 around 350-450ms today. For document summarization there's longer sequences, up to 1k tokens, that's more bursty and expensive.
[01:57] Priya: Cool, that helps. Do you have concurrent QPS or RPS numbers for peak?
[02:05] Maya: Peak is around 180 concurrent users right now in our production region. In terms of requests per second that's roughly 45-60 RPS with bursts up to 120 RPS during market opens.
[02:18] Alex: Good — so predictable baseline with short high spikes. That's the common Dedicated use case. Two immediate levers for you: reserved GPU pool sized for baseline, plus a burst pool or autoscale to absorb spikes.

[02:42] Priya: To clarify architecture — Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in a customer-dedicated cluster. You can configure a baseline commit and allow burst capacity that we can either route from our shared capacity or spin up over-provisioned instances depending on contract/tier. For private deployments we support VPC peering and on-prem variants too.
[03:02] Maya: When you say "route from shared capacity" — is that a live fallback to Redwood hosted? We have strict data isolation rules, some data cannot leave our VPC.
[03:12] Priya: Right. For customers with strict data residency we typically do one of two things: 1) have a Dedicated cluster with reserved GPUs in your VPC (we can deploy a private control plane and customer-managed networking), or 2) on-prem package where the runtime is in your network. The shared-hosted fallback would only be used if you opt-in and sign data processing agreements; otherwise we do local burst via cold-starting reserved instances or take burst from a dedicated reserved burst pool that sits in your tenancy.
[03:42] Tom: Ok that's important. We need KMS integration and full audit logs. Do you support BYOK/HSM?
[03:50] Jordan: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS providers and HSM for key wrapping. Audit logs are available per request and we can push logs to your SIEM. We also support SSO/SAML, RBAC, and can scope network egress rules.
[04:05] Tom: And SOC 2?
[04:08] Jordan: SOC 2 compliant; we'll share the report in the follow-up.

[04:30] Ethan: On sizing — how do you recommend we size GPUs? We use Llama-style models for many tasks and also a few LLMs with longer context for summarization.
[04:40] Priya: We typically size by baseline throughput needs and sequence-length distribution. For short chats (20-60 tokens) the throughput is high — more concurrent inferences per GPU. For long sequences you need more memory and will get fewer concurrent slots. Our sizing template asks for: p95 latency target, average seq length, peak RPS, and percent of long jobs. From what you said, baseline 45-60 RPS with 120 spikes is doable with 2-4 A100-ish equivalents for baseline and a burst pool of 1-2 extra GPUs, but we'll refine after we see your sample traces.
[05:12] Maya: What about cost — is reserved capacity billed monthly? And how does bursting get charged?
[05:20] Alex: Reserved capacity is a commitment (monthly/annual). Burst usage can be charged as overage at a different rate or pre-allocated as a burst pool with lower per-token rates. We can model both options; for finance teams we usually show a committed + overage scenario vs committed + burst-pool scenario.

[05:45] Ethan: We also care about KV cache/prefix caching for conversational state to lower cost. How does Redwood handle that on Dedicated?
[05:53] Priya: We support KV cache management and automatic prefix caching in the runtime. On Dedicated you get local cache per pod and can configure shared cache nodes for the cluster. Note that long-tail conversation caching requires memory planning — we'll include recommended cache sizing in the plan. Sometimes the transcription or docs call it "KV cash" in notes, ha.
[06:12] Ethan: Ha, yep.

[06:25] Maya: How quickly can autoscale/burst come up? We worry about cold-start latency for sudden spikes during market open.
[06:32] Priya: For bare autoscale it depends on provisioning time; if you're in the same cloud region we can cold-start instances in 2-7 minutes typically. For tight p95 SLOs we recommend a small warm pool and instant route-to-burst policy. That warm pool can be part of your reserved commitment or a small always-on buffer.
[06:50] Alex: Another option is continuous batching and request shaping to smooth spikes — reduces the need for big burst pools. We'll show you throughput improvements with batching for short token requests.

[07:08] Tom: From a compliance perspective, we need no outbound data egress to public internet, SAML with SCIM provisioning, and quarterly pen tests. Can Redwood support quarterly audits and provide evidence?
[07:19] Jordan: Yes. We'll provide pen test summaries, SOC2 report, and support an annual audit cadence. For SAML/SCIM we integrate with Okta and Azure AD.

[07:40] Ethan: For pilot scope — we'd like Redwood to run a benchmark with our sample prompts: 1) chat 20-60 tokens, target p95 <300ms; 2) doc summarization 800-1200 tokens, target latency p95 <2s; 3) nightly batch embedding workload. Can you support that?
[07:58] Priya: Absolutely. We'll need representative prompt traces and a small dataset. We typically run a 48-72 hour benchmark with synthetic and real traces to validate throughput and cost.
[08:08] Alex: We'll also include model variants and a quantized option to show cost/latency tradeoffs.

[08:20] Ethan: One more — fallbacks. If the Dedicated cluster is under load, what's our graceful degradation? We can't afford failed customer requests.
[08:28] Priya: Two-layer strategy: 1) route to a compatible, lower-cost model variant (e.g., quantized or distilled) within your Dedicated tenancy, and 2) if you opt-in, fallback to hosted in another region or dedicated overflow pool. We also support rate-limit shaped responses with clear error codes so your app can surface degraded responses gracefully.
[08:50] Maya: For networking — do you support VPC peering and private endpoints?
[08:55] Jordan: Yes, VPC peering, private link-style endpoints, and direct connect are supported. We'll provide the exact CIDR requirements and firewall rules in the network doc.

[09:10] Ethan: Sounds good. What's a typical timeline from contract to live pilot?
[09:15] Alex: For Dedicated in a cloud tenancy, provisioning can take 2-4 weeks after contract and network setup. On-prem deployments are longer (6-10 weeks) depending on site readiness. Pilot benchmark can run immediately after provisioning.
[09:28] Ethan: Good.

[09:40] Priya: Any questions about models — quantization or kernel selection?
[09:45] Ethan: We're already using int8 quantized models for some tasks. Curious how Redwood recommends quant profiles for latency-sensitive tasks.
[09:52] Priya: We'll recommend quant profiles per model and seq length; quantization helps but sometimes increases latency slightly for certain kernels. We'll show tradeoffs in the benchmark. Also we'll tune kernel selection in the runtime for your hardware.

[10:05] Tom: Ok last security question — data retention. We need logs kept for 12 months and an option to disable request metadata retention.
[10:13] Jordan: We can support customizable retention windows and redact request payloads on ingestion. We'll include those options in the security pack.

[10:28] Alex: Wrapping up: agreed actions are sizing + pricing, benchmark plan, and security docs. Any other blockers?
[10:35] Ethan: Not from ML side. We just need the numbers and a clear pilot scope.
[10:40] Maya: We'll review the network doc and get back with any questions.
[10:44] Tom: We'll need legal to review the DPA and DPAs for on-prem.
[10:48] Alex: Great — we'll send a follow-up email with attachments and proposed dates. Thanks all.

[11:05] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript contains minor transcription issues and conversational interruptions; speakers overlapped a couple times.
